title: Your daswandh, chosen
tomorrow: four things chosen. when in the day does the fifth one go?

lines: WHY GIVE ANY OF IT AWAY?
cards: A tenth of Simran's first real paycheck is less than a pair of sneakers and more than she wants it to be. She's spent the summer answering phones at her dad's trucking company, and the deposit just hit her banking app.
Harjit glances at the screen over her shoulder and says one word. Daswandh. She does the math on a napkin.
Then the question underneath the math: why give any of it away?

teach.b: Daswandh means a tenth, and in Sikh tradition it's the share of honest earnings given back, to the gurdwara, the langar, someone in need.

Its root in the Granth is a line of Guru Nanak's on Ang 1245, paraphrased: whoever eats from what they've honestly earned, and gives some of it with their own hands, recognizes the path. Notice the order.
Earn honestly first. Then give from your hands. The tenth itself comes from Sikh tradition; the Granth's line says some.
Here's a neighbor who knows the tenth well.
In Genesis, Jacob wakes from a dream at Bethel, sets up a stone, and makes a vow to God: "of all that thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto thee."
Jews and Christians both read that story, and the tenth runs on through the Torah, where Deuteronomy sets aside tithes for the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow.

That's shared ground worth telling a friend tonight: two traditions, each in its own words, counting a tenth back from what came to them. And an honest difference. In the Torah the tenth becomes law, with its uses named.

teach.h: A LAW IN ONE, A PRACTICE IN THE OTHER.
teach.b: Daswandh is a practice the Sikh tradition keeps, rooted in a line about honest work, and families decide where their share goes.
Simran writes two words on the napkin: langar, pantry.

how: Sikhs who keep daswandh set aside a share, traditionally a tenth of their earnings, for the gurdwara, langar, education or people in need; families decide how and where to give it, and some give time as well as money.

o: a tax the gurdwara collects from every family
the tenth day of a month, kept for fasting
the share of honest earnings you choose to give

games.q: a tenth, in two traditions — tap the pairs.
p: a tenth of honest earnings, given
earn honestly, give some by hand
Jacob vows a tenth at Bethel

in Genesis, Jacob vows to give God a tenth
of all that thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto thee.

games.q: your little brother earns his first lawn-mowing money and asks if he has to give some away. what fits daswandh?
o: a share of what he earned honestly, given gladly; tradition says a tenth.
nothing yet; daswandh is only for grown-ups with real paychecks.
all of it; the more you give away, the better a Sikh you are.
games.why: Ang 1245: earn honestly, then give some with your own hands. tradition counts that share as a tenth, and it starts with whatever you earn.

practice: Picture the share you'd like to give, from money or from time. Name the one thing most likely to stop you: forgetting, worry, a tight month. Then make the small plan that gets around it: how much, to whom, and on which day it goes.

wordCard.voice: Your daswandh: the share of what you honestly earn that you choose to give, traditionally a tenth.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a tenth part, the share of honest earnings Sikhs give.

carryVoice: For the road: my share, earned honestly and given from my own hands. The napkin says langar and pantry.
